title: Knowledge check: Handling Common Express Errors

questions.prompt: In Handling Common Express Errors, which statement best describes Malformed JSON?
options: Return the same success response for every request regardless of outcome.

questions.prompt: Which design rule is most appropriate when applying Handling Common Express Errors?
options: Centralize expected errors and forward unexpected failures to Express. Log enough structured context to diagnose a problem without recording credentials or unnecessary personal data; do not expose stack traces to clients.
Trust request fields and skip authorization to keep handlers small.
Suppress all errors without recording safe diagnostic information.
Assume that adding CORS makes private routes authenticated.
questions.answer_key: Centralize expected errors and forward unexpected failures to Express. Log enough structured context to diagnose a problem without recording credentials or unnecessary personal data; do not expose stack traces to clients.
questions.explanation: Centralize expected errors and forward unexpected failures to Express. Log enough structured context to diagnose a problem without recording credentials or unnecessary personal data; do not expose stack traces to clients.

questions.prompt: A change related to Handling Common Express Errors appears to work for one normal request. What is the strongest next verification step?
options: Test only one successful request manually and record no expected output.
Use production data to avoid building a small reproducible fixture.
Treat the page’s displayed reference output as proof that Node.js executed the code.
Use repeatable tests for a successful request and at least one invalid/boundary or dependency-failure case.
questions.answer_key: Use repeatable tests for a successful request and at least one invalid/boundary or dependency-failure case.
questions.explanation: Use repeatable tests for a successful request and at least one invalid/boundary or dependency-failure case.
